what_this_is: The first three pages describe the register as published. This page is the author's own view: what they would build, given what the audit found.

based_on.sources: The 2025 US federal AI use case inventory, read in full. The United Kingdom's recording standard, read as a published field template and not as records. The Government of Ontario's list, kept for one observation about supplier naming.
based_on.snapshot: A single point in time, each file recorded by SHA-256 hash in governance/data-provenance.md.

limits: Read from outside, with no access to how any agency works.
Built from what a published file shows, which is not everything an organisation knows.
Not tested against anyone who keeps a register.
This field set has not been used to record anything real. Every question on it answers something the audit found, and none of them has been put in front of a person asked to fill it in.
Nothing here compares one organisation with another. That is a choice, and it has a cost: the question a reader is most likely to arrive with is the one this project will not answer.

fields.name: Entry identifier
fields.records: A reference code that stays the same for this entry from one year to the next.
fields.finding: Of 3,611 entries, 706 carry no usable identifier, and the earlier year's list carries none for any entry, so no entry can be followed between the two.
fields.us_2025: Asks for one. It is filled on four fifths of entries, and 12 values appear on more than one row.
fields.uk: **Asks it.** Every record carries an ID, and a standard version alongside it.

fields.name: Date this entry was last checked
fields.records: The date a person last confirmed that this entry still describes the system.
fields.finding: Nothing in the register records when an entry was checked. Its single date field records when a system started running, which answers a different question.
fields.uk: **Asks it.** Three dates: when the record was completed, when it was last updated, and when it was archived.

fields.name: What changed since the last check
fields.records: Which of a named set of changes has happened since the entry was last confirmed: the responsible office, the model or its version, the data it draws on, what it is used for, or how far it acts without a person.
fields.finding: Five kinds of change would normally call for an entry to be verified again. No field in the register records any of them as a change, and one of the five is not present in the field set at all.
fields.uk: **Partly.** It asks for the model version in use and how the tool is maintained. Neither is a record of what changed since anyone last looked.

fields.name: Acts without a person reviewing the output
fields.records: Whether the system can carry out a decision or action without a person looking at its output first.
fields.finding: The 2025 federal register asks this only of its high-impact deployed entries. The UK standard asks it of every entry.
fields.us_2025: Not present in the 2025 field set.
fields.uk: **Asks it**, of every entry, in a field covering human decisions and review.

fields.name: Where a person reviews it
fields.records: The point in the process at which a person sees the output, if there is one.
fields.finding: The 2025 federal register asks this only of its high-impact deployed entries. The UK standard asks it of every entry.
fields.us_2025: Not present in the 2025 field set.
fields.uk: **Asks it**, in the same field, of every entry rather than of a subset.

fields.name: Impact classification, with an explicit option for not yet assessed
fields.records: How seriously the system is rated, including a value meaning no assessment has been made, so that an unassessed entry is distinguishable from a blank.
fields.finding: The classification field has four states in practice, and the fourth is that nothing was recorded: 426 entries carry no classification at all, which is more than the 110 assessed and set aside.
fields.us_2025: Asks it. The options do not include one meaning no assessment was made.
fields.uk: **Partly.** It asks whether an impact assessment was carried out and what the risks and mitigations are. It publishes no risk tier of its own.

fields.name: Withheld from public reporting, and on what ground
fields.records: Whether any part of this entry is held back from publication, and if so on what ground. Named in the direction the question is asked, so that an answer of no means nothing was held back.
fields.finding: The field asking whether an entry should be withheld is required, and is blank for 274 of the 445 entries flagged high-impact.
fields.us_2025: Asks it, and requires an answer.
fields.uk: Does not ask. What may be left out is set by a separate published scope and exemptions policy rather than by a field on the record.

fields.name: The nine oversight questions, each with its own explicit states
fields.records: Each carries its own answer, including one meaning the question does not apply. They are nine fields, not one.
sub_fields: Consultation with the people it affects
fields.finding: Of 445 high-impact entries, 126 answer all nine and 317 answer none, with two in between. The nine arrive together or not at all.
fields.us_2025: Asks all nine. Two of them offer a not-applicable option.
fields.uk: **Asks several of them**, of every entry rather than of a subset: human review, required training, appeals and review, impact assessment, risks and mitigations.

fields.name: What this entry counts as one of
fields.records: Whether this entry describes one system, or a class of common tools reported together, so that a reader knows what a count of entries is a count of.
fields.finding: The register publishes two routes that count different things and cannot be added: 3,611 systems reported individually, and 45 agencies reporting against 21 common tasks.
fields.us_2025: Implied by publishing two separate files, not recorded in either.
fields.uk: **Partly.** It separates the tool from the models inside it and asks about each, which settles the question differently rather than answering it.

fields.name: Who completed this entry, and when
fields.records: The office that filled this entry in, and the date it did so.
fields.finding: How completely an entry is filled in varies far less within one agency's submission than across the register, and the nine oversight fields arrive together or not at all. What produces that pattern cannot be read from the file, because it records nothing about who filled an entry in or when.
fields.uk: **Asks it.** A senior responsible owner is named, with the organisation and team, and the date the record was completed.

minimum_three.lead: These ten are a design, and nobody adopts a design. If only three of them are done, these three, in this order. The order is by what each one unlocks, not by how hard it is.

items.why_first: Nothing else can be checked over time without it. An entry that cannot be followed from one year to the next cannot be shown to have been kept up, however well the rest of it is filled in.
items.unlocks: Every other field becomes comparable across years. Duplicates become findable rather than guessable from wording.
items.cost: Low. The register already asks for one. What it lacks is a rule that the same entry keeps the same code, which costs a line in guidance rather than a change to any system.
items.evidence: 706 of 3,611 entries carry no usable identifier, and the earlier year's list carries none at all, so no entry can be followed between the two.
items.name: Entry identifier
items.records: A reference code that stays the same for this entry from one year to the next.

items.field: Date this entry was last checked
items.why_first: It separates a register from a list. Without it an entry written last month and one written years ago and never revisited are identical on the page.
items.unlocks: Anything about currency. A stale entry becomes visible without asking anyone, which is the only kind of check that scales.
items.cost: Low to record, higher to mean anything. The date is one field. Making it true requires somebody to do the checking, which is the operating model this field set does not describe.
items.evidence: The register records no verification date, no update date and no review date. Its one date field records when a system started running.
items.name: Date this entry was last checked
items.records: The date a person last confirmed that this entry still describes the system.

items.name: Explicit empty states on every field
items.why_first: It is third because the first two produce numbers, and numbers from a register with no rule for an absence cannot be read. This project published a figure that counted 218 entries the register never asked, and the reason it could is that a blank meant four different things.
items.unlocks: Every count becomes readable by someone who did not build the file. A question not put can be told from one unanswered, which no amount of care with a spreadsheet can recover afterwards.
items.cost: The highest of the three, and it is not technical. It means deciding in advance what answers a field may hold, which is a governance decision each time and cannot be delegated to whoever builds the form.
items.evidence: Three of the seven counting problems on the gaps page come from how an empty answer is recorded, and this project made the same mistake in its own published figures.
items.records: Every field distinguishes these states: answered, the question does not apply, not yet answered and withheld. No field records an absence as ordinary text.

minimum_three.after: What the three do not give you is any assurance that the register is kept. That is the page on keeping a register current, and none of the five mechanisms on it works without these three first.

convention.name: Every field records an empty answer the same way
convention.records: Every field distinguishes these states: answered, the question does not apply, not yet answered and withheld. No field records an absence as ordinary text.
convention.finding: Two fields store an empty answer as a pair of brackets a spreadsheet counts as content; words such as 'No' and 'Not available' record an absence in one field and a real answer in another; the development stage field offers four answers with no option meaning nobody filled it in; and a value the file uses appears nowhere in the document describing the field.
convention.us_2025: No single convention. Three of the seven counting problems on the gaps page come from how an empty answer is recorded.
convention.uk: **Settles it.** The standard publishes the answers each field may hold, and marks which fields are asked only under a condition, so a question not put can be told from one unanswered.

evidence.reads: of the entries the register asks the nine oversight questions of have all nine empty
evidence.caveat: The nine are asked only of high-impact entries that are deployed. A filled field shows information was provided, not that the practice is adequate.
The register asks for one, and permits agencies to remove the column from their own inventories.

evidence.reads: high-impact entries say nothing about whether they were withheld
evidence.caveat: A blank is not evidence anything was withheld. The field is required.

evidence.reads: entries carry no impact classification at all
evidence.caveat: No inference is drawn in either direction.

evidence.reads: of the entries the register asks for a date carry one that can be read reliably
evidence.caveat: It records when a system started running, not when the entry was checked. The register asks for it only of pilot and deployed entries.

evidence_withheld.name: How many entries resemble each other
evidence_withheld.why: It is three numbers, not one. The finding is that the count triples depending on where the line is drawn, so any single figure states the opposite of what was found.

evidence_withheld.name: How completeness varies within an agency against across the list
evidence_withheld.why: Its qualification shortens cleanly, but the figure does not stand alone: a median of two against fifteen means nothing without the setup that precedes it. Kept out of the strip for that reason, and linked instead.

timing.heading: Some of these blanks may be a clock, not a gap
timing.lead: A blank can mean nobody recorded the answer. It can also mean the work is under way and the answer does not exist yet. This project cannot tell those apart entry by entry, and the figures lean toward the second more than the headline suggests.
timing.reading: of every answer the nine oversight fields contain says a step is under way rather than finished.

the_clock.heading: What the memorandum says, and what it settles
the_clock.source: OMB Memorandum M-25-21, issued 3 April 2025. The register's own data dictionary cites it for the definition of high-impact AI, and the register's own README links to it.
the_clock.deadline: Section 4(a)(i) gives agencies 365 days from the issuance of the memorandum to document implementation of the minimum practices in Section 4(b) for high-impact uses of AI. That date is 3 April 2026.
the_clock.why_it_bears_on_these_fields: Section 4(b) is the list the nine fields come from. Pre-deployment testing, an impact assessment, ongoing monitoring, training for the people who use it, human oversight, a route of appeal, and consultation with the public are each named there. Two more of the nine sit inside the impact assessment itself: potential impacts at Section 4(b)(ii)(C) and the result of an independent review at Section 4(b)(ii)(F).
the_clock.what_the_register_says_about_its_own_tim: The register's README states that agency submissions were due to OMB on 22 December 2025 and that the public reporting deadline was 28 January 2026. Both are earlier than 3 April 2026. It also states that updates to the repository are processed on a rolling basis, and this project downloaded the file on 22 September 2026.
the_clock.rule_set_in_advance: If the deadline comes before the snapshot, a blank is read as a gap. If it comes after, a blank is read as a clock that has not run out.
the_clock.answer: The deadline comes before the snapshot. The file was downloaded more than five months after 3 April 2026, so by the rule set in advance these blanks are read as a gap rather than as work that was not yet due.
the_clock.what_would_change_it: The deadline also comes after the date agencies submitted, and the repository takes updates on a rolling basis. So an entry submitted in December 2025 and never touched since would still be inside its clock. Telling those entries from the rest needs a record of when each entry was last updated, and the register has no such field. That is this project's third finding, and it is the reason the second field in this set exists.
the_clock.what_it_still_does_not_show: The memorandum requires the work to be documented and the agency to be ready to report it through any of three routes, of which this inventory is one. A blank here is not evidence about the work itself.

timing.consequence: Read the blanks as what reached the file on the day it was downloaded, not as work that was not done.

not_covered.heading: What this field set does not do
not_covered.lead: These ten questions describe what a register should record. They do not describe how one is run, and a register that is not run is a document rather than a control.

missing.name: A named person accountable for each entry
missing.why: A field with no owner is nobody's to keep current.
missing.finding: How completely an entry is filled in varies far less within one agency's submission than across the register, and the register records nothing about who filled an entry in.
missing.covered_by: NIST AI 100-1, GOVERN 2.1, which asks that roles and responsibilities be documented. The UK standard names a senior responsible owner on the record itself.

missing.name: What forces an update, and how often one is due
missing.why: Two of the ten ask when an entry was last checked and what changed. Neither makes anyone check it.
missing.finding: The register records no verification date, no update date and no review date, and no field records any of the five changes that would normally call for an entry to be checked again.
missing.covered_by: NIST AI 100-1, GOVERN 1.5, which asks that periodic review be planned and its frequency decided. Annex VIII of the EU regulation requires registered information to be kept up to date after it is first entered.

missing.name: Approval gates tied to buying and starting a system
missing.why: A register filled in after the fact records decisions rather than shaping them.
missing.finding: The register is filled in once a year on a submission deadline. Nothing in the file ties an entry to the point at which a system was bought or switched on.
missing.covered_by: Article 49 of the EU regulation, which requires registration before a system is placed on the market or put into service. The entry is a condition of use rather than a record made afterwards.

missing.name: A state for a system that has been switched off
missing.why: Without one, a register grows and never empties.
missing.finding: The development stage field offers four answers and no option meaning nobody filled it in. Entries not carried forward from the earlier year cannot be told from entries that were withdrawn.
missing.covered_by: Annex VIII, Section A, point 7 of the EU regulation, whose status field includes no longer on the market, no longer in service, and recalled. NIST AI 100-1, GOVERN 1.7, asks for a process for taking a system out of use.

missing.name: A link from each answer to the evidence behind it
missing.why: Every field here records a claim. None records where the claim can be checked.
missing.finding: A filled oversight field shows information was provided. Nothing in the register points at the document behind it, so no answer can be checked from outside.
missing.covered_by: Annex VIII, Section C of the EU regulation, where a public body registering a use gives the address of the provider's entry and summaries of two named assessments.

not_covered.coverage: There is also a limit no register design can solve from outside. A published list shows what an organisation wrote down. It cannot show systems nobody declared, or the AI features that arrive inside software bought for something else. Both are outside anything this project can see.
not_covered.comparators_lead: The comparison in the field set is the United Kingdom's recording standard. Three other published texts bear on what a register records and how one is kept. Two were read for this section, from the publisher's own text, downloaded and recorded by hash like every other source. One was not, and the reason is stated.

comparators.name: The European Union's rule on entering AI in a public database
comparators.what: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, read in the consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. Article 49 says who has to register and when. Article 71 sets up the database and says which parts of it the public can see. Annex VIII is the field list.
comparators.why: It is a register with a different purpose. Registration comes before use rather than after it, and the regulation decides who has to appear on the list, which neither the US list nor the UK standard does.
comparators.what_it_settles: Four of the five things this field set leaves out are written into its field list or its timing.

comparators.name: The United States framework for managing AI risk, NIST AI 100-1
comparators.what: A framework published free by the National Institute of Standards and Technology. Its GOVERN function sets out what an organisation should have in place around AI, rather than what a record should contain.
comparators.why: It treats the inventory as a control rather than a document. GOVERN 1.6 asks that mechanisms be in place to inventory AI systems and be resourced according to risk. GOVERN 1.5 and 1.7 cover review and taking a system out of use.
comparators.what_it_settles: The part this field set leaves out, which is how a register is kept up rather than what it records.

comparators.name: The international standard for managing AI, ISO/IEC 42001
comparators.what: A published standard describing how an organisation should run its AI oversight. An organisation can be checked against it by an outside auditor.
comparators.why: It is sold rather than published. Every other source named on this site was downloaded, hashed and recorded, and nothing here is written from a text this project has not read. A mapping built from other people's summaries of a standard would be the one thing the rest of this project does not do.
comparators.what_it_settles: Not stated, because it was not read.

not_covered.consequence: Treat this as a proposal about what a register records, traced to one published file and compared against one published standard. It is not an operating model. Two published texts that do cover the operating side were read and are mapped against it above.

oversight_denominator.heading: Correction, 2026-09-30
oversight_denominator.text: An earlier version of this site counted the nine oversight questions across all 445 entries marked high-impact and reported 317 with none answered. The register's own dictionary asks those nine only of high-impact entries that are deployed. Counted against the 227 entries it does ask, the figure is 101, or 44.5%. The gap is smaller and it is still there. Every other field's denominator was then checked against the dictionary. The same fault was found in the one date field and corrected with it. The check is recorded in governance/corrections.md.

oversight_base.heading: Correction, 2026-09-30
oversight_base.text: Every per-question figure on this page, and the reading of what the answers say, was divided by all 445 entries flagged high-impact. The register asks these nine only of the 227 that are also deployed. Measured against those, the share of answers saying a step is under way is 32.7% rather than 16.9%, the share saying a step was done is 20.5% rather than 10.7%, and each question is answered on about 55.1% of entries rather than about 28.5%. The picture is less empty than this page showed. This is the third figure on this site corrected for the same reason, and the check that now covers the class is in governance/corrections.md.

date_denominator.heading: Correction, 2026-09-30
date_denominator.text: The one date field was reported as a share of every row in the register. The dictionary asks for it only of entries at the pilot and deployed stages. Usable dates were published as 31.7% of the register and are 67.6% of the 1480 entries the register asks.

reading.heading: How to read these numbers
reading.lead: Everything on this site is counted from one published file. These five rules apply to every figure on every page, so they are stated here once rather than repeated under each one. A finding carries only what qualifies that finding.

rules.rule: A filled field shows that information was provided, not that the practice is adequate. An empty field is not evidence that the practice is absent.
rules.applies_to: Every completeness figure, and the nine oversight fields in particular.

rules.rule: Every figure describes what reached the file, not what any organisation did.
rules.applies_to: Every figure. This project reads a published file from outside and has no access to how any organisation works.

rules.rule: A share is divided by the entries the register asks, which is often fewer than the whole file. Where the two differ, both are published and the narrower one is the one describing a question with no answer.
rules.applies_to: 22 of the register's 31 fields, which are required only under a stated condition.

rules.rule: A published list can only show what was declared. Nothing here says anything about systems nobody wrote down.
rules.applies_to: Every count of entries. Undeclared systems are outside anything this project can see.

rules.rule: Nothing here compares one organisation with another, and no entry shown was picked out. Where a single entry appears, the rule that selected it is printed beside it.
rules.applies_to: Every page. There is no ranking, score or league table anywhere on this site, and that is a deliberate choice with a cost.

about.lead: A portfolio project by Sana Ahmad.
about.text: It asks what an AI use case register should record, and answers it by auditing a real one rather than reasoning from first principles. Every figure, decision rule and safeguard is open, including the ones this project got wrong and corrected.

panel_one.selection_rule: The first entry in the file's own order among those the register asks the nine oversight questions of and that carry no answer in any of them.
panel_one.why_this_entry: Selected by rule, not chosen. The first entry in the file's own order among those the register asks the nine oversight questions of and that carry no answer in any of them. 100 other entries meet the same rule and would produce the same picture, so nothing here is about the organisation that filed this one.
panel_one.rule: Every value here is read from the published file. Nothing is inferred, estimated or filled with a plausible answer. Where the source collects nothing, the row is marked as such. Where the source asks and this entry is empty, the row is marked differently, because those are different facts.

panel_two.system: A fictional tool that drafts replies to passenger complaints
panel_two.label: Fictional throughout. No real organisation, no real system, no real data. It exists to show the field set filled in.
panel_two.reading: Every box on this form is resolved. Most carry an answer. Among the nine oversight questions, one is not put to this entry and one has been put and has no answer yet.
